title: Bless the year
hookLine: a prayer for the year's harvest and livelihood

lines: A LINE CHANGES IN EARLY DECEMBER.
A BLESSING ABOUT MAKING A LIVING.
cards: Here's a strange fact about Jewish prayer outside the land of Israel. On a date in early December, Jews in New York, London and Buenos Aires change one line of the weekday Amidah.
Not on a Jewish holiday: on a date tied to an old way of counting from the autumn equinox. In Israel the change comes weeks earlier. The line is about rain.
But it sits inside a blessing about something everyone, everywhere, worries about: making a living.

teach.b: The ninth blessing is called birkat hashanim, the blessing of the years. It says: bless this year for us, and all its kinds of produce, for good. Satisfy us from its goodness, and bless our year like the good years.
Blessed are You, who blesses the years. In the rainy season, people ask: give dew and rain for a blessing. In the dry season, simply: give blessing.
A week ago you met the rain line in Gevurot. That one praises God who makes the rain fall. This one actually asks for it.

teach.h: ASKING FOR RAIN, NOT ONLY PRAISING.
teach.b: In Israel, the asking begins in the autumn, on the seventh of the month of Cheshvan; the Mishnah explains the delay: so that the last pilgrim from the festival could get home, as far as the river Euphrates, before the rain.

teach.h: ISRAEL IN AUTUMN, ABROAD IN DECEMBER.
teach.b: Outside Israel, Jews follow the Babylonian Talmud's reckoning, which is why the date lands in early December.
The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, also says why this blessing is ninth: against people who drive prices up, because of a line in what it counts as the ninth psalm, break the arm of the wicked.
Even a blessing about harvests keeps one eye on fairness. If you don't farm, the blessing still fits.
Some add their own words here about work and income, what Jews call parnassah, livelihood. Like the good years: a modest request. Not a fortune.
A year that feeds you, the way the good ones did.

how: Birkat hashanim is the ninth blessing of the weekday Amidah; Jews in Israel add the request for dew and rain from the seventh of Cheshvan, Jews elsewhere from early December, and some add personal requests for livelihood within it.

games.q: you're a rabbi in the land of Israel. the festival has just ended and pilgrims are walking home. when should people start asking for rain?
o: immediately, the day the festival ends.
about two weeks later, once pilgrims are home.
games.why: the Mishnah, following Rabban Gamliel, waits until the seventh of Cheshvan, so the last pilgrim can reach the Euphrates before the rains.

practice: Picture your work, whatever it is, a job, a business, school, caring for kids or parents, looking for work, and the year ahead of it, the good months and the slow ones.
Hold one modest hope for it: not a windfall, just a year that feeds you and the people who depend on you. If you pray, you can ask in the blessing's own words, like the good years.

wordCard.voice: Parnassah. Livelihood — what the ninth blessing, birkat hashanim, asks for alongside rain and harvest: a year that feeds you, like the good years.
